Baselau u.a., Leer 1987, p. 13 Despite numerous unsuccessful events and circumstances (the plague of 1625, 1708, 1711, stationing of the foreign army during the Swedish and Russian wars in the years 1758-1762), in the Early Modern period, Ostróda developed in economic and demographic terms. In 1740 it had 698 inhabitants, and after half a century — in 1787-1539 people lived there*?. At the beginning of the 18^ century it did not differ from other towns of similar size in Prussia, except the burghers' painful duty of quartering the army“. An important event for the history of Ostróda was a fire which broke out on 21 July 17885'. The fire started in an old malt house and quickly spread to the adjacent buildings and the castle where the powder stored there exploded. Within a few hours almost the whole town had burnt down, including 164 buildings which mainly belonged to burghers, theso-called German church, the town hall, the tannery and the previously mentioned malt house. The only places which survived the fire were the vicinities of the Kościelna Gate, the Polish church, two schools, the Łazienna Gate and over 40 buildings in the Łazienne suburbs. There were not many fatalities (4), but hundreds of the 1539 inhabitants had to leave Ostróda for good. In order to prevent the town's disappearance the Prussian king helped the inhabitants of Ostróda; so did the inhabitants of Miłomłyn [German: Liebemühl] and Morag [German: Mohrungen] and other German centres. Bricks from the city walls and towers were used to reconstruct Ostróda. The concept of the urban development of Ostróda had not changed until WWII.

Barkowsky's plan of August 1788 is the basic source of knowledge about the spatial layout of Ostróda only in the late Early Modern period, because after the fire the earliest spatial layout was not reconstructed completely. Nevertheless, the layout of the town is not easy to reconstruct. On the basis of the city plans, J. Müller assumed that after the fire the building development in Ostróda had been somewhat freer, which changed its spatial layout$^. According to his hypothesis — rejected by all historians9before the fire, Ostróda had a quadrangular marker square constituting the extension of Langegasse street which, in turn, was the extension of Hauptgasse street. On the market square there was a town hall; the only thing we know about what it looked like before the fire is that it was a massive building with a tower, a clock and a “banner” presenting a rider. Next to the town hall there were the so-called stall sheds$9. Owing to a lack of parallelism of the arms constituting the delta of the Drweca river, after the fire Ostróda had almost a rhomboid shape with the dimensions 460x350x240x100 m. The market situated along the river had a trapezoid shape and was 48x75x45x70 m in size; it consisted of two parts: the first was later called the Old Market (Alter Markt), and the other the New Market (Neuer Markt) — the latter was a nearly perfect isosceles triangle. Barkowsky did not give the name Alter Markt; he just drew there Langgasse running along the northern frontage of the market, where in the central market place he marked the old town hall, for the new town hall was not finished until 179257. The old town hall looked different from the building which was erected earlier and survived until WWII, for it had a shape of a rectangle the longer side of which ran along the market square. Fig. 5. A weekly market in the Old Town (Alter Markt), the building of the Town Hall in the background in 1928, Der Kreis Osterode Ostpreußen in Bildern, At that time Ostróda had three gates. North of the Łazienna Gate (Badertor) there ran a route in the direction of Mitomtyn and Elblag. Barkowsky's plan shows two suburbs: the Łazienne suburb (Badervorstadt) and the Fiugajny suburb (Figehnen), both located on both sides of the crossing of what are now Olsztyńska street and K. Pulawskiego street. In the area situated far from the fork of the river there were about a hundred buildings at the end of the 18% century. The movement from the town to the east and to the south-east to Kajkowo [German: Buchwalde] and Olsztynek [German: Hohenstein] took place through the Kościelna Gate (Kirchentor, Katarinnentor in 1603), the name of which came from the adjacent Polish and German churches. Near the road to Olsztyn, in the north-east there started to extend the suburbs of Pauza (near what is now Gizewiusza street) and

Senden (in the area of what is now Polna street and Olsztyńska street). The third gate, the so-called Garncarska Gate (Topfertor) led southwards to two routes: one in the direction of Lubawa [German: Löbau in Westpreußen] and Iława, and the other (of secondary importance) to Olsztynek. The suburb of potters existed in the area of what is now Spichrzowa street (in the past Bahnhofquerstrasse) — and on the plan we can find flats of craftsmen, a pottery stove and a brickyard. To the west, beyond Barkowsky's plan, in Jaracza street (Jakobstrasse) there was a settlement of brick makers. Through the Water Gate [Polish: Furta Wodna] on the western side burghers moved to a castle moat to collect water. People could also collect water from the southern branch of the Drweca river. Quite a few burghers resided in the areas located on the north-west part of the town, near the mill? which belonged to the starostwo. On Barkowsky's plan there is Wodna street (Wasserstrasse), but the same name was held by a short street in the eastern part of the town which connected Tylna street (Hintergasse) with the church. Wasserstrasse — the fragment of present Mickiewicza street from the junction with Stapińskiego street up to Olsztyńska streetwas marked out in 1789. The creation of the street is associated with the first attempt to modernise the spatial layout of Ostróda, the aim of which was to combine the town with the northern suburbs and to allow transit communication bypassing the town centre. It is highly probable that at the same time present Drwecka street (Drewenzstrasse) was marked out for the same reason. Thanks to this, Ostróda acquired another ring road, which brought the inhabitants of the Pausen and Seden suburbs closer to the town centre. Barkowsky's plan reveals that land estates of burghers were situated south of Pauzeńskie (Pausen) Lake and at Drweckie Lake, south of the Pausen river (Pauzen Fliess). The plan bears the names of 18 owners of land, six of whom sound Polish. Between the southern branches of the Drweca river there were small buildings and gardens. Not all the plots on the plan bear their numbers — buildings which fail to bear numbers are the houses in the southern part of the town, near the branch of the Drweca river, and in the north in Tylna street (Hintergasse). This may be evidence that the buildings were still destroyed after the fire or that nobody lived there. In the area formerly surrounded by the city fortifications there were ten streets marked out.

The period of the Napoleonic wars worsened the demographic situation of Ostróda. The evidence for this is Rehefeld's plan of the town of the years 1807-1818 which presented Ostróda in hydrographic-topographic terms*?. The plan does not show any spatial development of suburban areas. Many buildings were converted into warehouses and the Kościelna Gate was demolished. From 21 February to 1 April 1807 in the castle of Ostróda there were the headquarters of the Napoleonic army. Emperor Napoleon did not think highly of the town and called it a "poor village"? After the Napoleonic wars had ceased in 1815, the administrative reform took place in Prussia thanks to which Ostróda became the capital of the county. The first landrat of Ostróda was Wilhelm Leopold Kóhn von Jaski. From 1818 within the chief county office of Ostróda [Landratsamt], the town developed on the territory of the so-called Pausen island (Insel im Pausen bei Osterode) situated north of the city walls on the patrimony between the Drweca river from the south to Drweckie Lake from the east and Pauzeńskie Lake from the north. According to the cartographic sources of the years 1822 and 1827", in the southern part of the territory there were quite a few houses built. Three bridges (Amtsbrücke, Baderbrücke, Grünebrücke) led to the island from the south. The area included two cemeteries (Evangelical and Jewish), a pasture for horses (Rofigarten) and a mill. Fig. 6. Vogelsang, Leer 1984, p. 12 At the beginning of the second half of the 19” century south of the centre of Ostróda there was a southern branch of the Drweca river which was not filled in until about 1899. In the period of time the northern part of the town developed the demolition of the medieval walls allowed it to be extended down to the river line. The most interesting are the comments connected with Koenig's plan of 1850 concerning eleven forts around Ostróda located in strategic points near roads leading up to the town. The plan assumed erecting the fortification camp of the Rogniata type, with sparse defence elements such as forts, battery emplacements, entrenchments and a redoubt. As no information about the fortifications has been preserved, so it may be concluded that it was a preliminary plan. Its original version

was to be found in the general staff of the army, which allows us to suppose that there was a plan to convert Ostróda into a stronghold constituting an element of the system of the Prussian fortifications (Giżycko, Grudziądz). However, the peaceful times after 1850 meant that the project was given up”?. Until 1945 the centre of the western part of the market square was occupied by the two-storey town hall, the layout of which is known to us from Ulfert's plan of 18507. Other important public buildings included the two-storey building of the county court erected in 1900 and extended in the years 1932-1933. About 1900 visible spatial changes in Ostróda may be noticed, which resulted from the intensive processes of modernisation taking place in East and West Prussia. The town was inhabited by over 13,000 people. There were 668 houses built in the town, which compared with the year 1858 (282 houses) constituted a significant increase in their number. Two factors affected the development of Ostróda in demographic and spatial terms. The first factor was the construction of the Elblag-Ostróda canal (Oberlándisches Kanal) in 1852 which joined Drweckie Lake and Jeziorak Lake with Elblag. The idea to construct the canal appeared in the 1830s when it was intended to activate economically small towns in East Prussia; the advocates of the investment were a town councillor of Ostróda Eisengráber and a town-councillor of Elbląg Georg Jacob Steenke”*. From 1856 steamships arrived in Ostróda and the coast of Drwecka Bay was gradually developed and extended. The process sped up when cargo transport intensified at the turn of the 19*—20^ centuries. On the coast there appeared four navigation points; the harbour included also warehouses, a shipyard and a steam mill of Miller and Herrenberger'*. The other factor was the development of communication infrastructure. After the development of paved roads such as the one to Piławki (Pillauken) (1845) and Olsztynek (1857) it was decided to build a railway Torui-Ostróda-Olsztyn-Wystrué (Insterburg). At the end of the century, after a half-kilometre-long embankment through Drweckie Lake had been made, in 1899 the railway reached Mitomlyn. At the beginning of the 20^ century Ostróda became a significant railway junction in the southern part of East Prussia after railway connections to Morag, Olsztynek and Działdowo had been introduced. The building of the railway station was erected in Ostróda in 1870; on its northern side a big railway base was created, while further on the west a cargo railway station was built. Most buildings of the railway base (i.e. repair workshops) were located in 11 Listopada street (Wilhelmstrasse). Gradually both sides of Dworcowa street leading up to the promenade and the centre were developed. As railways tracks divided the town, crossings had to be built across the tracks.

In 1895 the Fountain of Three Emperors was built next to the town hall. It commemorated three rulers from the Hohenzollern dynasty: Wilhelm | (1871—1888), Frederick IIl (12 March-15 June 1888) and Wilhelm Il (1888-1918). The fountain, designed by an artist from Berlin Arnold Kunne (1866-1942), became the symbol of the town reproduced in numerous postcards. It survived the war; since 2004 it has been referred to as the Fountain of the European Unity — the images of the emperors were replaced by the Ostróda coat of arms, the coat of arms of am Harz (Ostróda's twin town) and the symbol of the European Union. Another important factor facilitating the development of the town was the garrison. On the plans from the beginning of the 20^ century in the north of Ostróda, east of the Evangelical cemetery, there are the so-called Alte Infanterie Kaserne created in the mid—19" century where the infantry military units were stationed (in the years 1898—1913 the Second Battalion of 152 Infantry Regiment under the name of the Teutonic Order). The barracks also referred to as Bergkaserne were converted into a housing estate after WWI. In the south of the town, near the road to Olsztynek (Hohenstein) Neue Infanterie Kaserne was built, which is also called the "red barracks"; later, in the interwar period it was referred to as Grolmankaserne — from the name of the general, the commander of the Prussian army, Karl Georg von Grolman (1777—1843), the patron of the First Pausen Infantry Regiment No. 18. It was a very modern barracks complex linked with the hospital built at the junction of Spangenbergstrasse (at present the fragment of Grunwaldzka street from the junction with Czarnieckiego street to the junction with Drwecka street) and Drewenzstrasse (now the fragment of Drwęcka street to the junction with Olsztyńska street down to the exit of the road to Tysiaclecia square).

They were referred to as Artillerikaserne; they were surrounded by a fragment of present Pienieznego street from the junction with Ko$ciuszki street to the junction with 21 Stycznia street (Artilleriestrasse), part of Władysława Jagiełły (Hubertusstrasse), Kościuszki street (Olgastrasse) and a fragment of Czarnieckiego street from the junction with Kościuszki street to the exit from the town in the direction of Kajkowo (Kaiserstrasse). Apart from buildings devoted to soldiers there were also flats for officers and the commissariat. Thanks to further investments in the area of Zeromskiego street, Kopernika street, Piłsudskiego street, Jagiełły (Blücherstrasse, Mackensenstrasse, Grolmannstrasse, Litzmannstrasse) the empty space between both complexes of barracks was developed. In the northern part of the town, at Pauzeńskie Lake, there were such important objects as the water supply system (1903), a power plant (1911), gasworks (1905), a slaughterhouse (1893) and a cattle market. The sanitary condition of Ostróda improved after a water tower (Wasserturm) was erected in 1903; the water supply system was developed, and the sewage system was extended (1904). One Evangelical cemetery was situated in Herdera street (Herderstrasse) and present Sienkiewicza street (Schillerstrasse), while the other one in the north-eastern corner of the town next to the road to Lubajny [Lubainen]. The Catholics were buried in the cemetery in Kaiserstrasse (now the fragment of Czarnieckiego street from the junction from Kościuszki street to the exit road from Ostróda to Buchwald (Kajkowo). At the beginning of the 20^ century on the site of the southern branch of the Drweca river, which had been filled in, Szkolna street was marked (Schulstrasse). At the same time the area on the southern side of railway tracks to Olsztyn had already been developed. At the end of the 19^ century and at the beginning of the 20^ century in Ostróda there appeared new buildings for educational and church institutions. In the building at the junction of Pienieznego street (Artilleriestrasse) and 21 Stycznia street (Graudenzer Strasse) Mádchen-und-Knaben-Volksschule Süd was set up and a tourist youth hostel was opened nearby. The most important educational institution in the town was Kaiser-Wilhelm-Gymnasium, which in 1907 was moved to a new building in Drwecka street (Hindenburgstrasse). In today's Jana Pawła Il street (Seminastrasse) the building of the Royal College for Teachers was erected, while in Stapińskiego street (Schulstrasse) a public school for girls was built (Mádchenschule-Nord). In Ostróda there was also a vocational school (Fach.u. Berufschule) in Kardynała Wyszyńskiego street (Albertstrasse). Other important cultural institutions were two theatres — Luisen Theater and Elisenhof located in Drwecka street (Drewenzstrasse)'6.

Most inhabitants of Ostróda at that time (about 8396) were Evangelicals. The first Jews appeared in Ostróda probably in the first years of the 18^ century, but even in the mid—19'^ century their number did not exceed 4% of the total population”. The main temple of the united and uniting church in Ostróda was a medieval church in the Old Town reconstructed in 1897. The sacral topography of the town failed to include a small "Polish" Evangelical church which was demolished in 1912. On its site a pastor's house was built (it has not survived, either). In 1909 on the hill on the corner of Herdera street (Herderstrasse) and today's Sienkiewicza street (Schillerstrasse) another Evangelical church was constructed with a forty-five-metrelong tower??; the church now belongs to the Evangelical-Methodist Parish Church of Divine Grace in Ostróda. Prior to WWI the Catholic church erected in the years 1856— —1857 was extended (the tower was added in 1903); there were about 15% Roman Catholics at that time. The synagogue in the Moorish style was built in Ostróda in 1893 in Olsztyńska street (Gartenstrasse); it was burnt down by the Nazis during the so-called Crystal Night on 9-10 November 193879. In the 1930s in Rossgartenstrasse (now the fragment of Mickiewicza street from the junction with Olsztyńska street to the mill and the lock of the Elblag-Ostróda canal (Oberlandisches Kanal)) a Masonic Lodge "Humanitati" was situated. Baselau u.a., Leer 1987, p. 87 In the meantime, individual quarters of Ostróda were being developed; new housing estates were created (e.g. in Luther v. Braunschweigstrasse). The outskirts of the city, both in the north and in the south, were not a densely built-up residential area. Among public utility buildings we can distinguish a county hospital at the junction of Drwęcka street (Drewenzstrasse) and former Sendenhauptstrasse, which in now a fragment of Olsztyńska street from the junction with Gizewiusza street to the exit from the town. In the centre, in Seegang and Wasserstrasse streets there was a building of the imperial post office (1897)%. The starost's office was situated (1878) north of the old Teutonic castle, near today's fragment of Mickiewicza street from the junction with Stapińskiego street to the junction with Olsztyńska street (Wasserstrasse).

The social-economic changes in Ostróda at the turn of the 19% and 20% centuries reflect the results of the Prussian statistics. At the beginning of the 1870s the population of the town reached 4,500 people, whilst in 1919 it went up to 15,000*'. However, it must be concluded that the social, political and economic changes did not entail an increase in the percentage of the Polish, Catholic population coming from Lubawa and Warmia [Ermland]. Polish Catholics had been living in Ostróda since the Middle Ages, but they belonged to the poorer social strata usually living in secondary streets and suburbs. Most of them were Masurians who had been coming from Masovia since the end of the 14" century to settle down in the southern part of the Teutonic state, the Duchy of Prussia; they spoke the language of their ancestors, which they heard at weekly fairs and markets: five horse and five cattle fairs, and two stall fairs. About 1700 near Ostróda there ran a kind of German-Masurian language borderline*?. Many activists propagated Masurian consciousness among people. One of them was Gustaw Gizewiusz® (born 1810, died and buried in Ostróda in 1848); together with Christopher Celestine Mrongovius he wrote a memorial to King Frederick Wilhelm IV concerning the maintenance of the Polish language in schools and the Church. The activity of another propagator Jan Karol Sembrzycki, the editor of the periodical Mazur printed in the printing shop belonging to a German Karol Edward Salewski. Nevertheless, all those attempts did not prevent the Germanisation process (German schools, Church, the military service in the German army). In the period of WWI, during the battle of Tannenberg on 26-30 August 1914, the headquarters of General Paul von Hindenburg and his general staff were situated in Ostróda's School named after Augusta Wiktoria. After the military actions had finished, the school took another name: Hindenburg-Schule (now Primary School no. 2 under the name Gustaw Gizewiusz in Ostróda). Luckily, Ostróda avoided destruction during the war, unlike other towns e.g. Dzialdowo. After the war, the political patronage of Ostróda county and seven other Masurian counties was to be resolved by plebiscite as stipulated in the Treaty of Versailles. The population of Warmia [Ermland], Masuria and Powisle had to decide whether the territories should be incorporated into the new Polish state or should be left within the borders of East Prussia. The plebiscite was held on 11 July 1920 under the auspices of the League of Nations. The Polish party was not properly prepared for it. High financial investment, good organisation and abuse by the German party made the result of the plebiscite a foregone conclusion. In Ostróda merely 17 people voted for Poland. From the whole county of Ostróda (where 97.896 of the population voted for East Prussia) only three villages were incorporated into Poland: Lubsztynek, Napromek and Groszki**.

In the interwar period Ostróda was the capital town of the county. The county of Ostróda occupied a territory of 1551 km? and consisted of 167 settlements, including four towns: Ostróda, Olsztynek, Milomlyn and Dabrówno (Osterode, Hohenstein, Liebemühl, Gilgenburg).The rising demand for electricity in Ostróda led to the establishment of a power distribution company (Elektrizitátswerk by Das Ostpreufbenwerk) in 1921. The town was slowly becoming a tourist destination offering three bathing beaches at Drwęckie Lake to which led three roads referred to as Seegang |--III. Even more tourist were attracted after the erection of the National Monument (Nationaldenkmal) near Tannenberg, where in 1934 Marshall Hindenburg was buried. The Nazi authorities brought about the change of street names in the town. More important streets took names with propaganda overtones: Seminarstrasse was changed into Adolf-Hitler-Strasse, Wasserstrasse into Strasse der SA, Hauptstrasse became Hermann-Górring Strasse. On the eve of WWII Ostróda, the seventh largest town of East Prussia, had almost 20,000 inhabitants. In 1935 in the garden area in J. Stapińskiego street (Schulstrasse) a new fire station and several houses were built. On the former training yard on the road to Warlin a new housing estate was constructed. Next to it, before WWI (1912) an airport was built for flights from Germany to East Prussia; however, the regulations of the Treaty of Versailles hindered its development and the territory is now occupied by Plebiscytowe Housing Estate. Die Madchen-Schule was situated on the corner of Drwecka street (Friedrichstrasse) and Stapińskiego street (Schulstrasse), while Die Knabenschule in Olsztyńska street (Ludendorfstrasse), next to the cemetery. Inhabitants of Ostróda enjoyed spending their time in a municipal park established between the northern coast of Drweckie Lake and present 3 Maja street (Bismarckstrasse). In the park there was the Tower of Bismarck (Bismarckturm) with a restaurant; from the top of the tower there stretched a beautiful panorama of the "pearl of Oberland"**. West of the municipal park there was a bathing resort with separate places for ladies, families and gentlemen. Fig. 10. The Red Army entered Ostróda in the night of 21/22 January 1945. Practically, no fighting had taken place, but the Soviet soldiers burnt down as much as 64-70% of Ostróda's buildings, which ruined most of the town. Of about 1300 buildings, 720 were totally destroyed, and a large part of the remaining buildings was not suitable to live in. Until 1955 not a single new house was built in Ostróda. In the later period in some parts of the town it was forbidden to redecorate buildings, for according to the urban development plan new buildings were destined to be incorporated in the old housing system. The comparison of the situation of Ostróda in 1788 and in 1945 reveals how many lives were lost and how huge a catastrophe the war was. Most people from Ostróda had left the town before the Red Army entered Ostróda. Most of them started a new life in Germany cultivating the memory about their town of origin and the achievements of the previous generations in Ostróda and the adjacent area”. Merely 2,000 inhabitants decided to stay in Ostróda. Their lives became unbearable in the subsequent months due to famine, rape and robberies**; many of them, including Masurians, who had survived the first weeks, decided to escape. The Soviet commander of Ostróda Colonel Iwan S. Konstantinow, who at first did not allow representatives of the Polish authorities to enter Ostróda, had a negative attitude towards Polish settlers in Ostróda; he supervised the dismantlement of various facilities and their transport to the USSR. On 26 May 1945 Ostróda was officially passed to the Polish administration represented by the starost S. Cendrowski. Gradually, public utility institutions such as schools, offices, a hospital, an army unit and others started operating in the town. It took about 20 years to reconstruct the population potential of Ostróda (back to the condition in 1938). About 3096 of new inhabitants of Ostróda were the so-called repatriates from the former Borderland of the Rzeczpospolita*?. At the beginning of the 1970s the economic stagnation made a significant number of people leave Ostróda for other parts of Poland or the

Federal Republic of Germany, which caused a negative migration balance**, The demographic and economic situation improved after the meat processing plant in Morliny had been opened in 1975. This investment entailed the introduction of public transport in Ostróda. Nowadays, Ostróda occupies a territory of 1409 ha and is inhabited by almost 35,000 people. Its area increased in 1977 after the incorporation of Nowosiółki, Wałdowo, Morliny (excluding the State Agricultural Farm — PGR), Kajkowskie Lake and Zajerze. Despite the losses from the final stage of the war, Ostróda has maintained its old spatial layout and remained the administrative centre, the site for the local authorities (the starostwo), industrial and educational centre; the military garrison also survived the war*'. The old centre of Ostróda was not reconstructed — modern blocks of flats were built in the area in the 1960s and 1970s. In 2004 there was commissioned a new town centre situated on the western side of the former Old Town, in the square between Mickiewicza-Zamkowa streets and Plac Tysiąclecia Państwa Polskiego, where buildings are stylised to look like historical tenement houses. In this attractive complex combined with the park there are offices, shops and a bank. Demographic changes after WWII had a limited influence on the change of the functions of the public utility buildings which had survived the war. The Housing Cooperative "Jedność" which was established in Ostróda on 15 March 1958 built a big housing estate in Władysława Jagiełły street and 21 Stycznia street. New housing estates were also built in Grunwaldzka street, Plac Tysiąclecia and Kopernika street. In the north-west end of the town, near Partyzantów street the Drwęckie estate of detached houses was created; at Smordzińskie Lake — the estate of Osiedle Młodych (the Housing Estate of the Young), while on the western side a complex of prefabricated-sections houses called Osiedle Jaracza. Another important investment was the construction of the Warsaw-Gdansk ring road which took over the transit movement. Some of the buildings of the barracks are being gradually transformed to be used by civilians. The present local authorities of Ostróda emphasise the importance of the development of tourism, sport and recreation. Numerous lakes are an undeniable advantage of the town — five lakes are situated within the borders of the town, while another ten very near. The town also has a harbour of three inland canals which are the longest in Poland (129.8 km).
